title: Reconstructive ladder: skin grafts versus flaps

guidelineVersions: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery, 28th edition (2023)

related.why: Excision of the skin lesion that created this defect
Wound healing and abnormal scarring once a graft or flap has healed

brief.scenario: Ms Sophie Marchant, 49, has a soft-tissue defect on her lower leg after excision of a skin lesion. The wound bed has exposed tendon.
brief.task: Discuss how you would reconstruct this defect and answer the examiner's questions on grafts and flaps.

beforeYouWalkIn.frame: Assess the defect and the patient first, then work up the reconstructive ladder from simplest to most complex.
beforeYouWalkIn.trap: Saying a graft can cover any wound, or that a flap is always the better choice.
beforeYouWalkIn.firstMove: "I'd assess the wound bed, exposed structures, vascularity, contamination and her overall condition first."

flow: Why a flap is needed here

grid.label: Systematic assessment of the defect
grid.fail: Jumps to naming a technique without assessing the wound bed, exposed structures, vascularity, contamination or patient factors.
grid.pass: Assesses the defect, wound bed, exposed structures, vascularity, contamination and the patient's overall condition before choosing a technique.
grid.high: Links each assessment finding to a specific reconstructive option, rather than listing factors in the abstract.

grid.label: The reconstructive ladder
grid.fail: Cannot describe the ladder, or treats it as a rule that the simplest option is always correct.
grid.pass: Describes the ladder as moving from simpler techniques to more complex reconstruction as the defect demands.
grid.high: States the ladder is a framework, not a rule: the simplest technique giving durable functional cover is chosen, not automatically the lowest rung.

grid.label: Skin graft limits
grid.fail: States any wound can take a skin graft, including one with exposed tendon or bone.
grid.pass: States a graft needs a vascularised wound bed and cannot reliably take over poorly vascularised structures such as bare tendon, bone or some implants.
grid.high: Explains why: a graft has no blood supply of its own until it 'takes' from the bed, so it depends entirely on that bed for survival.

grid.label: Why this wound needs a flap
grid.fail: Says a flap is always better than a graft, without linking the choice to this wound.
grid.pass: States a flap brings its own blood supply and can cover a wound a graft cannot, such as exposed tendon here.
grid.high: Adds that a flap also restores bulk and contour over the tendon, which a graft alone would not.

grid.label: Graft and flap classification
grid.fail: Cannot distinguish split-thickness from full-thickness graft, or name any flap type.
grid.pass: Distinguishes split-thickness from full-thickness skin graft, and names local, regional and free flaps.
grid.high: Adds tissue composition options (skin, fascia, muscle or composite) and how donor-site morbidity and vascular anatomy influence the choice.

grid.label: Choosing the reconstruction and involving plastics
grid.fail: Does not mention involving plastic surgery, or picks a reconstruction without weighing function, contour, sensation or donor-site morbidity.
grid.pass: Chooses the simplest reconstruction giving durable functional coverage, weighing patient factors and reconstructive goals, and involves plastics for a complex defect.
grid.high: Explains that involving plastics early, before further debridement changes the defect, keeps the widest range of options open.

failures.move: Choosing a technique before assessing the wound bed, vascularity and patient factors.
failures.consequence: The reconstruction may fail because it does not match the wound it is covering.

failures.move: Placing a skin graft directly over exposed tendon.
failures.consequence: The graft will not take, leaving the tendon exposed and at risk of desiccation and infection.

failures.move: Assuming a flap is always the right choice, even for a simple superficial wound.
failures.consequence: Unnecessary donor-site morbidity and operative time for a wound a graft would have closed just as well.

failures.move: Not involving plastic surgery for a complex defect with exposed tendon.
failures.consequence: Options may be lost, or a technique beyond the operator's training is attempted.

recovery.when: You can't decide between a graft and a flap
recovery.line: I'd ask whether the wound bed can support a graft, or needs a flap's own blood supply.

recovery.when: Asked what happens if the graft fails
recovery.line: I'd expect exposed tendon to desiccate, and would plan for flap coverage as a backup.

knowledge.fact: The reconstructive ladder moves from simpler to more complex options; the simplest technique giving durable functional cover is chosen, not automatically the lowest rung.
A skin graft needs a vascularised wound bed and cannot reliably take over bare tendon, bone or some implants.
A flap carries its own blood supply, restoring both coverage and bulk where a graft cannot survive.
Split-thickness and full-thickness grafts differ in dermal thickness and donor-site healing; flaps can be local, regional or free, and vary in tissue composition.

recall.think: Can this wound support a graft, or does it need a flap's own blood supply?
recall.say: "This defect needs a flap: the exposed tendon won't support a graft."
do: State the ladder is a framework, not a rule
Assess wound bed, vascularity and patient factors
Name the graft or flap type and why
recall.trap: Assuming any wound bed, including bare tendon, can take a skin graft.
recall.finish: Simplest reconstruction giving durable functional cover; flap where a graft cannot survive.

partner.opening: Ms Marchant, 49, has a soft-tissue defect after excision of a skin lesion, with exposed tendon at its base. "What options are available?"

reveals.trigger: Candidate asks about the wound bed or contamination
reveals.finding: The wound bed is otherwise clean and well vascularised; no residual tumour at the margins.

reveals.trigger: Candidate asks about her general health
reveals.finding: She is a fit non-smoker with no diabetes or peripheral vascular disease.

push.question: Would you use a skin graft?
push.expect: Needs a vascularised bed; can't reliably cover bare tendon.

push.question: When would you need a flap?
push.expect: When a graft can't survive; a flap brings its own blood supply.

push.question: Why can't a skin graft reliably cover exposed tendon?
push.expect: A graft depends on the wound bed for vascular support, which bare tendon lacks.

curveballs.prompt: The patient asks why you wouldn't just use the simplest option.
curveballs.safeAnswer: The ladder is a framework: choose the simplest technique giving durable functional cover, not automatically the lowest rung.

curveballs.prompt: The registrar suggests a full-thickness graft over the tendon.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Any graft, split or full-thickness, still needs a vascularised bed; bare tendon won't reliably support either.

curveballs.prompt: Could you use a local flap instead of a free flap?
curveballs.safeAnswer: Yes if local tissue with adequate vascularity is available nearby; otherwise regional or free flap options are considered.
Donor-site morbidity is part of the reconstructive choice, and plastics can advise on minimising it.
